# Job 18 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Bildad's second speech is the shortest of the three friends'第二轮 discourses but arguably the most brutal. He abandons all earlier hints of comfort (cf. Job 8:20–22) and delivers an unrelentingly graphic description of the fate of the wicked — every detail aimed, however unjustly, at Job. Commentators across traditions agree that while Bildad's theology of retribution is *generally* true, his application to Job is profoundly wrong.

---

## v. 1–3: Bildad's Opening Rebuke

**v. 1 — "Then Bildad the Shuhite replied:"** This is Bildad's second speech in the cycle (the first being Job 8). He is now more exasperated and aggressive than before.
— Gill, Intro: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/18.htm

**v. 2 — "How long until you end these speeches? Show some sense, and then we can talk."** Bildad charges Job with endless, unproductive talk. The plural "ye" (in the Hebrew) may address Job as representative of a class, or possibly include others present who may have murmured support.
— Enduring Word (Guzik), citing Bullinger: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-18/
— Gill notes Bildad's impatience: "he falls with great fury upon him": https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/18.htm
— Matthew Henry says Bildad was "weary of hearing others speak, and impatient till it came to his turn": https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC18018.HTM

**v. 3 — "Why are we regarded as cattle, as stupid in your sight?"** Bildad resents Job's earlier remark sending them to the beasts for instruction (Job 12:7) and Job's claim that God has hidden understanding from them (Job 17:4). Bildad considers this a grave insult.
— Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/18.htm
— Enduring Word (Trapp): "Bildad herein sinned against the law of love": https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-18/

---

## v. 4: "You Who Tear Yourself in Anger"

**Traditional reading:** Bildad turns Job's own words back on him. Job had said God tore him in anger (Job 16:9); Bildad retorts that Job is actually tearing *himself* apart through his own rage and impatience. The rhetorical questions — "shall the earth be forsaken on your account, or the rocks be moved?" — mean: Do you really expect God to overturn the fixed moral order of the universe just for you?
— Enduring Word (Guzik, citing Andersen and Morgan): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-18/
— Matthew Henry: "Anger is a sin that is its own punishment. Fretful passionate people tear and torment themselves." He adds that Bildad accuses Job of expecting Providence itself to change its settled course for one man: https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC18018.HTM
— Gill: "He teareth himself in his anger" means Job tears his own soul. "Shall the earth be forsaken for thee?" — must the world be depopulated or God drop his government because of one man? https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/18.htm
— Pulpit Commentary: Bildad thinks Job's repeated assertion of innocence "aims at the subversion of the moral order of the world": https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/18.htm
— Dunagan: Bildad complains that Job insists God change the nature of the universe to accommodate his claim of being an exception: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/job-18.html

---

## v. 5–6: The Lamp of the Wicked Extinguished

**v. 5 — "Indeed, the lamp of the wicked is extinguished; the flame of his fire does not glow."** The "lamp" and "fire" symbolise prosperity, joy, and life. Bildad asserts with absolute confidence that the wicked always lose their light in this life. Gill clarifies this is *outward* prosperity, not spiritual light (which, once given, cannot be lost). Matthew Henry notes the wicked's light is "but a spark… a little thing and soon extinguished … not the light of the Lord."
— Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/18.htm
— Matthew Henry: https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC18018.HTM
— Enduring Word: "Bildad's concern was to establish in Job's mind the absolute certainty that every wicked man gets paid in full, in this life" (Smick): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-18/

**v. 6 — "The light in his tent grows dark, and the lamp beside him goes out."** The "tent" suggests domestic life; Bildad pictures the home itself going dark — a terrifying image in the ancient Semitic mind. The Pulpit Commentary notes this is a favourite biblical image (cf. Job 21:17; 29:3; Psalm 18:28; Proverbs 13:9) and that Arabs say "Fate has put out my lamp."
— Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/18.htm
— Dunagan: The term "tent" indicates the patriarchal era: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/job-18.html

---

## v. 7–10: The Dangerous Path — Six Hunting Images

**v. 7 — "His vigorous stride is shortened, and his own schemes trip him up."** The confident, swaggering stride of the prosperous man is cut short. Ellicott: "His giant strides … he shall be the victim of his own devices." Bildad's point: the wicked are brought down not by external misfortune but by their own counsels — an insinuation that Job's calamities are self-inflicted.
— Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/18.htm
— Gill: "His own counsel shall cast him down" — as with Ahithophel and Haman: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/18.htm

**vv. 8–10 — "For his own feet lead him into a net … A trap seizes his heel; a snare grips him. A noose is hidden in the ground, and a trap lies in his path."** Bildad uses six different Hebrew words for hunting devices (net, mesh, trap, snare, noose, pitfall). Andersen (cited by Guzik) notes that precise identification of each is impossible, but the cumulative effect is overwhelming: the world is a network of snares for the wicked man. Crucially, *his own feet* lead him there — Bildad blames the victim.
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-18/
— Matthew Henry sees three agents at work: Satan preparing destruction, the sinner preparing his own destruction, and God preparing destruction. "The sinner by his sin is preparing the fuel and then God by his wrath is preparing the fire": https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC18018.HTM
— James Smith (Precept Austin): "Satan uses every possible means to prevent that man who 'knows not God' from escaping … But it is with 'his own feet' that a man walks into the Devil's net": https://www.preceptaustin.org/job-commentary-james-smith (section "Job 18:5-18. TERRIBLE PROSPECTS")
— Dunagan: "The world of God is one network of snares for the wicked man" (Davidson): https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/job-18.html

---

## v. 11–12: Terrors and Depleted Strength

**v. 11 — "Terrors frighten him on every side and harass his every step."** Bildad mirrors Job's earlier complaint of being attacked on every side (Job 16:9–14) and turns it into evidence of guilt. Ellicott renders "shall chase him at his heels." Matthew Henry sees this as the terrors of conscience: "He that carries his own accuser, and his own tormentor, always in his bosom, cannot but be afraid on every side."
— Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/18.htm
— Matthew Henry: https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC18018.HTM
— Pulpit Commentary likens the pursuing terrors to the *Erinnyes* (Furies) of Greek mythology: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/18.htm

**v. 12 — "His strength is depleted, and calamity is ready at his side."** Some commentators (e.g., Ellicott) note that "strength" could refer to the firstborn son (as in Genesis 49:3), but most take it literally. "Calamity is ready at his side" personifies destruction as a hungry predator waiting to pounce. The KJV renders it "destruction shall be ready at his side"; RV has "destruction shall be ready for his halting."
— James Smith (Precept Austin): "Destruction shall be ready for his halting" — keeping step with the man who does not know God, watching for the moment death causes him to stumble: https://www.preceptaustin.org/job-commentary-james-smith

---

## v. 13: "The Firstborn of Death"

**v. 13 — "It devours patches of his skin; the firstborn of death devours his limbs."**

This is one of the most debated phrases in the chapter.

**Traditional reading:** Bildad directly alludes to Job's skin disease. "The firstborn of death" means the most terrible and deadly disease — death's strongest child. Just as a "firstborn" son inherits the father's prime strength (Genesis 49:3), so this disease embodies death's fullest destructive power. The Pulpit Commentary identifies it specifically as elephantiasis (what Job likely suffered). Whedon agrees: "If the Arab deems 'fevers to be the daughters of death,' the terrible elephantiasis may well be called his firstborn."
— Barnes (via StudyLight): "the most fearful and destructive disease that death has ever engendered": https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/18-13.html
— Cambridge Bible: "the strongest child of death" or "deadliest death"; cf. "firstborn of the poor" = the very poorest (Isaiah 14:30). Arabs call deadly diseases "daughters of death": https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/18-13.html
— Whedon: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-18.html
— Kingcomments: "the most powerful of death … Bildad says that Job has been beaten with the most terrible and devastating diseases": https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/job-18.html

**Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes / Bible Odyssey):** One alternative view (noted by John B. Burns in *Vetus Testamentum*, 1987) is that "the firstborn of death" may refer to Namtar, the Mesopotamian god of pestilence and vizier of the underworld — a deity figure from the cultural background of the ancient Near East.
— Constable (via StudyLight): https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/18-13.html

**Protestant devotional reading:** James Smith (Precept Austin) spiritualises it: "Spiritually the firstborn of death is unbelief, that forerunner of eternal separation from God … which devours all strength for the service of Christ, roots up all real confidence before God, and brings the soul into the bondage and dread of the king of terrors."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/job-commentary-james-smith

---

## v. 14: "The King of Terrors"

**v. 14 — "He is torn from the shelter of his tent and is marched off to the king of terrors."**

**Traditional reading (virtually unanimous across traditions):** "The king of terrors" is a personification of Death itself. Ellicott calls it "perhaps the most remarkable personification of unseen forces to be found in the Bible." The Pulpit Commentary specifies it is death, not Satan. Matthew Henry expands: "Death is terrible to nature … but to the wicked it is in a special manner the king of terrors, both as it is a period to that life in which they placed their happiness and a passage to that life where they will find their endless misery." He then contrasts the believer's experience: through Christ, "this king of terrors becomes a friend and servant!"
— Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/18.htm (see also https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/job/18-14.htm)
— Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/18.htm
— Matthew Henry: https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC18018.HTM
— Enduring Word (Guzik): notes a parallel to the Canaanite deity Mot (Death) "whose gullet reaches from earth to sky — the devouring deity" (Smick), but also cites an old Irish tombstone that addresses Death as a tyrant: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-18/
— Geneva Study Bible gloss: "he shall be brought to the king of terrors": https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gsb/job/18.htm

**No significant denominational disagreement** was found on this phrase. All consulted sources identify it as death personified.

---

## v. 15: Fire and Brimstone

**v. 15 — "Fire resides in his tent; burning sulfur rains down on his dwelling."**

The reference to "brimstone" (burning sulfur) is universally seen as alluding to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24) — a sign of divine judgment. Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik) adds that it may also refer to "an ancient custom of fumigating houses with brimstone, in order to purify them from defilement" after a corpse had lain there.
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-18/
— Ellicott: "probably an allusion to the cities of the plain (Genesis 19)": https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/18.htm
— Matthew Henry: "Brimstone shall be scattered upon his habitation, rained upon it as upon Sodom": https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC18018.HTM

**An alternative reading noted by Dummelow:** Some read v. 15a as "Lilith shall dwell in his tent" — Lilith being a nocturnal demon/vampire figure known in Mesopotamian folklore. This reading comes from a variant understanding of the Hebrew. However, most English translations (including BSB, KJV, ESV) do not adopt this.
— Dummelow: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/job-18.html

---

## v. 16: Roots Dried Up, Branches Withered

**v. 16 — "The roots beneath him dry up, and the branches above him wither away."**

Bildad returns to his favourite tree metaphor from his first speech (Job 8:11–19). The image of total destruction — below and above, roots and branches — signifies complete annihilation of the wicked man and his family line. Ellicott notes the "tacit allusion" to the destruction of Job's own children, already accomplished. The Pulpit Commentary observes that an imprecation on the sarcophagus of Eshmunazar (a Phoenician king) reads: "Let him have neither roots below nor branches above" — showing this was a common ancient curse-formula.
— Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/18.htm
— Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/18.htm
— Matthew Henry draws a contrast: "Those who take root in the earth may expect it will thus be dried up; but, if we be rooted in Christ, even our leaf shall not wither": https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC18018.HTM
— Spurgeon, in a sermon on Job 19:28 ("the root of the matter"), notes how Bildad used this tree metaphor twice (Job 8 and Job 18) to accuse Job of being a hypocrite — an assault Job parried by insisting "the root of the matter is found in me": https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons27/sermons27.xxiv.html

---

## v. 17–19: No Memory, No Offspring, No Survivor

**v. 17 — "The memory of him perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the land."** In the ancient Near East, to have one's memory blotted out was among the most dreaded of fates. Job had pled for the earth to testify on his behalf (Job 16:18–19); Bildad counters that the wicked man's memory simply vanishes. Matthew Henry: "All his honour shall be laid and lost in the dust … The memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot (Prov. 10:7)."
— Matthew Henry: https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC18018.HTM
— Gill: "he shall have no name in the street … no good name among men; if ever his name is mentioned … it is with some brand of infamy": https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/18.htm

**v. 18 — "He is driven from light into darkness and is chased from the inhabited world."** The wicked man is expelled from the land of the living. Gill notes some read the Hebrew as "they shall drive him" — referring to God, or to angels (good or bad) driving him into eternal darkness.
— Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/18.htm (see also https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/job/18-18.htm)

**v. 19 — "He has no offspring or posterity among his people, no survivor where he once lived."** This is arguably Bildad's cruelest blow. Job had lost all ten children (Job 1:18–19). Bildad implies this proves Job is among the wicked. Guzik calls it "singularly cruel." Andersen (cited by Guzik): "Bildad gives a transparent allegory which is singularly cruel in its obvious reference to Job's bereavement. The last state, having no offspring, descendant or survivor, is the worst." Matthew Henry counters: "All that are written childless are not thereby written graceless; there is a name better than that of sons and daughters."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-18/
— Matthew Henry: https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC18018.HTM
— Ellicott: "He shall have neither his own son's son among his people, nor any remaining, where he sojourned": https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/18.htm

---

## v. 20–21: Universal Horror and the Final Verdict

**v. 20 — "Those in the west are appalled at his fate, while those in the east tremble in horror."** The wicked man's doom is so shocking that it produces awe and terror in all who witness it — both "those in the west" (lit. "those who come after," later generations) and "those in the east" (lit. "those who went before," earlier generations). Ellicott: "He shall stand forth as a warning and monument to all."
— Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/18.htm
— Matthew Henry: "Those that see it are affrighted, so sudden is the change, so dreadful the execution": https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC18018.HTM

**v. 21 — "Surely such is the dwelling of the wicked and the place of one who does not know God."** Bildad's concluding verdict: not only is Job among the wicked, but he is one who "does not know God" — a devastating charge against a man whom God Himself called "blameless and upright" (Job 1:1). The Pulpit Commentary notes that Bildad "designedly uses the singular here" — he intends this entire terrible picture to represent Job personally. G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Guzik): "This is a tremendously powerful delineation of the way of wickedness. Again we have to say — all true, and therefore to be taken to heart; but not all the truth, and therefore of no meaning in the case of Job."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-18/
— Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/18.htm
— Matthew Henry: the beginning of wickedness is ignorance of God (wilful ignorance), and its end is utter destruction. "Vengeance will be taken of those that know not God, 2 Thess. 1:8": https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC18018.HTM
— Bridgeway Bible Commentary: "His fate becomes a lesson to all who would oppose God": https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/job-18.html

---

## Denominational Distinctives and Other Views

### Across Protestant Traditions: Broad Agreement

The consulted sources from Baptist (Gill, Spurgeon, Smith), Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik), Methodist (Whedon), Anglican (Ellicott), and older Evangelical/Puritan (Matthew Henry, Pulpit Commentary) traditions show **no substantial doctrinal disagreement** on Job 18. All agree that:

1. Bildad's description of the wicked's fate is *theologically true* in its general contours — the wicked do face judgment.
2. Bildad's *application* to Job is profoundly wrong and cruel — Job is not a wicked man.
3. The chapter illustrates the danger of applying general theological principles without pastoral sensitivity to a particular person's suffering.
4. "King of terrors" = death; "firstborn of death" = a deadly disease (especially Job's elephantiasis).

### Spurgeon (Baptist) on the Tree Metaphor

Spurgeon, in a sermon on Job 19:28, reflects on how Bildad used the tree/root metaphor twice (Job 8 and 18) to attack Job as a hypocrite. Job's reply — "the root of the matter is found in me" — is, for Spurgeon, the key to the whole exchange: Job could admit the branches were gone but insisted the root of faith remained. This refutes Bildad's logic.
— https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons27/sermons27.xxiv.html

### Modern Scholarship: Mesopotamian Background

- **Namtar / "firstborn of death":** John B. Burns (*Vetus Testamentum*, 1987, cited by Constable) proposed that the "firstborn of death" reflects Namtar, the Mesopotamian god of pestilence. This is a minority view among evangelical commentators but illustrates the ancient Near Eastern cultural background of the book.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/18-13.html

- **Lilith in v. 15:** Dummelow notes that some read "Lilith shall dwell in his tent" rather than "It shall dwell in his tent, because it is none of his." Lilith is a nocturnal demon/vampire in Mesopotamian folklore. Most English translations do not adopt this reading, though the RV margin acknowledges it.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/job-18.html

### Catholic and Orthodox Views

No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on Job 18 was found from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search results. The Church Fathers (e.g., St. John Chrysostom, St. Gregory the Great) wrote on Job, but accessible online commentaries from these traditions did not appear in the search results for this specific chapter.

### Reformed, Lutheran, Methodist Distinctives

No dedicated Reformed (Ligonier, Monergism, TGC), Lutheran (LCMS, 1517.org), or specifically Wesleyan/Methodist (Seedbed) commentaries on Job 18 appeared in the searches. The absence of disagreement in the available sources suggests that Job 18 is not a passage where these traditions diverge significantly — the chapter's meaning turns more on pastoral application (how we speak to sufferers) than on doctrinal distinctives.
